newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire officials despair as army fails in east.
newsitem.headline: Zaire officials despair as army fails in east.

text.p: Authorities in Zaire are worried that the country's demoralised soldiers are helping a Rwandan-backed rebel offensive by alienating local populations before rebels arrive, senior government sources say.

Given the utter failure of the army to beat the rebels who have seized a swathe of eastern Zaire since October, some government officials privately see negotiations with guerrillas as Zaire's only way out.

"It is the same now as it was in Goma and Bukavu more than a month ago," a senior government official said. "The rebels announce they are coming days in advance. The soldiers loot the town and disappear hardly putting up resitance."

A similar scenario is playing out in major Zairean towns in the path of the rebel advance in the east, such as Kisangani and the strategic mineral town of Kindu. Rebels say they have taken Kindu and are about to capture Kisangani, Zaire's fourth city.

The chief editor of the local Catholic church radio station in Kisangani told Reuters that there was no sign of rebels within 50 km (35 miles) of the city, but the army itself was proving to be the problem.

"The local population is calm, and the high command has called on the radio for calm among the soldiers. But the problem of uncontrolled elements is still with us," editor Jose Menga said by telephone from Kisangani on Thursday.
Deserting soldiers routed in the eastern front where rebels launched a campaign in October have been arriving in Kisangani in stolen aid vehicles.
There have been constant reports of rape and looting by the soldiers both in the town and on approach roads from the eastern battlefront.

Aid workers who left the city earlier this week said the military is spending more time and energy trying to control and disarm demoralised deserters who no longer obey any authority, than they do in preparing for a rebel attack.

It is only in the South Kivu region near the town of Fizi that the army claims to have won back rebel-held territory. A relief official in Kinshasa said that troops in that region had been paid and fed in order to boost morale.
Most Zairean troops have not been paid for several months and looting is an institutionalised compensation.
Zaire has also ceded territory on the Uganda border, some of it occupied by Ugandan troops chasing their own guerrilla foes.

After a Central African summit in neighbouring Congo last Tuesday, Zaire's interior minister said the regional leaders backed Zaire and would not expect Africa's colonial frontiers to be re-arranged by belligerent states.

"All the Central African states are agreed that the stability of Zaire is essential to the countries of Central Africa," Kamanda wa Kamanda said in an interview broadcast on state television on Thursday.
But while the government continues to put a brave face on the crisis in public, one despairing senior official said that in private alarm bells are now ringing among ministers.

"Zaire is so huge and some people have been saying to themselves that the fighting is still 2,000 km (1,200 miles) from Kinshasa. But if it were to reach Kinshasa no one knows how bloody it could be, or how many scores there would be to settle," said the senior official, who asked not to be named.
Some officials see negotiation now as the only way out.
"Perhaps the one way to win back a better position from which to start negotiations is to hire mercenaries. Because our own army is proving ill-equipped for the job," said the same senior official.
President Mobutu Sese Seko has been absent from Zaire throughout the crisis. After cancer treatment in Switzerland, he is now at his villa in the French Riviera.
